paras: The whitecapping of Clifford Williams was a night raid and written warning against a Black man near Bryant Station, Saline County, Arkansas, in August 1890. About twenty armed men seized him to see whether the women of a white household would identify him as an accused assailant, and released him when they did not. A notice signed "Committee" then ordered him to leave within ten days, and he moved away.

Williams, "a colored man," said he had lived there twenty-six years. On the night of July 31, the dispatch said, "some colored men" assaulted Mrs. Baldwin at the home of Bob Ferguson, a white man near Bryant.

At about 11 o'clock on a Saturday night, apparently August 2, about twenty men surrounded Williams's house and demanded to be let in. When he refused, they smashed in the door, bound and blindfolded him, and marched him to Ferguson's home. There "the ladies failed to recognize him as the negro who had made the assault," and the gang "reluctantly" let him go.
The following Monday he found a notice on his gate post, dated August 2 and signed "Committee," ordering him out within ten days, with drawings of a hanging man and a coffin.

Warned by his employer that he might be shot from ambush, Williams moved to another district. He went to Little Rock to consult federal and state authorities and said the raiders were all "prominent Democrats," some of whom he recognized.

The only report found is a Little Rock dispatch of August 7, printed on the Wheeling Daily Intelligencer's front page on August 8 under "Warned to Leave." It printed the notice in full but hedged Williams's story, calling it a case of "bulldozing in which he poses as the victim." No Black-press coverage of the episode was found.

The dispatch gives his first name as "Gil. ford" in its text, while the notice is addressed to "CLIFFORD WILLIAMS." The gang appeared to be hunting the assailant, but Williams, who had lately declared for the Union Labor ticket, blamed his politics, a claim resting on his word alone.

reader.title: Whitecapping of Clifford Williams
bases: A night gang of about 20 armed men broke into Williams's house and released him unharmed, and the lasting act was a notice signed 'Committee', with drawings of a hanging man and a coffin, ordering him to leave within ten days, which he obeyed (A1).

About 20 men acting with no lawful authority seized Williams to see whether he was the man accused of an assault, but released him when he was not identified; he was threatened with hanging but not killed (A1).
The only report is one Little Rock dispatch printed in the Wheeling Intelligencer, resting mostly on Williams's own account to a reporter (A1).

accounts.label: Williams's account (Little Rock dispatch)
accounts.gist: A gang of Democrats broke in, took him to Ferguson's, freed him when the women did not recognize him, and then posted a notice ordering him out; he attributed his unpopularity to his intention to vote the Union Labor ticket.

framing.detail: The Wheeling paper ran the dispatch under 'Warned to Leave' and 'The Blood Curdling Notice', printing the notice in full, while the dispatch hedged Williams's account ('claims to have lived', 'poses as the victim').

versions.value: Clifford Williams (as printed in the notice)

conflicts.note: The same article gives both spellings; the notice text reads CLIFFORD and the 'Gil. ford' form may be an OCR or typesetting break.

versions.value: Suspicion of the July 31 assault at Ferguson's (the gang took him there for identification)
Political: Williams called the men prominent Democrats and linked his unpopularity to his Union Labor vote

conflicts.note: Both come from the same dispatch; the political motive is Williams's own claim.
